questions.question_text: What is the primary aim of focused antenatal care?

choices.text: To provide care only when pregnancy complications develop
To promote maternal and fetal wellbeing through individualised, evidence-based care and early identification of complications
To ensure that every pregnant woman delivers by caesarean section
To replace skilled care during labour and childbirth

questions.rationale: Antenatal care promotes the health of the pregnant woman and fetus through preventive interventions, screening, education and management of identified risks. It also supports birth preparedness and timely referral when complications arise.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an important component of the initial antenatal assessment?

choices.text: Obstetric history, medical history, physical examination and relevant investigations
Assessment of the newborn's feeding pattern
Routine administration of antibiotics to every pregnant woman
Assessment of cervical dilatation in every pregnant woman

questions.rationale: The initial antenatal assessment establishes the woman's baseline health status and identifies factors that may affect pregnancy. It includes a comprehensive history, physical examination and appropriate laboratory screening.

questions.question_text: Which investigation is routinely used to screen pregnant women for anaemia?

choices.text: Haemoglobin estimation or full blood count
Electroencephalography
Electromyography
Visual field assessment

questions.rationale: Haemoglobin estimation or a full blood count helps identify anaemia during pregnancy. Early detection allows appropriate investigation, treatment and follow-up to reduce maternal and fetal complications.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a danger sign during pregnancy that requires urgent assessment?

choices.text: Mild nausea during early pregnancy
Vaginal bleeding
Gradual abdominal enlargement
Increased appetite

questions.rationale: Vaginal bleeding during pregnancy may indicate miscarriage, placental complications or another serious condition. The woman requires prompt assessment and appropriate management rather than routine reassurance.

questions.question_text: Which event marks the beginning of the first stage of labour?

choices.text: Delivery of the placenta
Onset of regular painful uterine contractions associated with progressive cervical effacement and dilatation
Complete delivery of the fetus
Onset of breastfeeding

questions.rationale: The first stage of labour extends from the onset of true labour to full cervical dilatation. True labour is characterised by regular uterine contractions associated with progressive cervical change.

questions.question_text: At what cervical dilatation is the cervix considered fully dilated for the second stage of labour?

choices.text: 4 cm
6 cm
8 cm
10 cm

questions.rationale: Full cervical dilatation is 10 cm and marks the beginning of the second stage of labour. The second stage continues until the complete birth of the baby.

questions.question_text: What is the main purpose of active management of the third stage of labour (AMTSL)?

choices.text: To prevent prolonged pregnancy
To reduce the risk of postpartum haemorrhage
To prevent all perineal tears
To accelerate cervical dilatation

questions.rationale: AMTSL is used to reduce the risk of postpartum haemorrhage, particularly bleeding associated with uterine atony. It includes administration of a prophylactic uterotonic and appropriate management of placental delivery according to current protocol.

questions.question_text: What is uterine involution?

choices.text: The progressive return of the uterus towards its pre-pregnancy size after childbirth
The enlargement of the uterus during pregnancy
The expulsion of the fetus during labour
The production of breast milk after delivery

questions.rationale: Uterine involution is the physiological process through which the uterus decreases in size after childbirth. Effective uterine contraction and tissue changes help reduce postpartum bleeding and restore the uterus towards its pre-pregnancy state.

questions.question_text: Which description correctly identifies lochia rubra?

choices.text: White or creamy discharge occurring in the later puerperium
Red or blood-stained vaginal discharge occurring during the early postpartum period
Green, foul-smelling vaginal discharge indicating normal recovery
Clear fluid discharged before the onset of labour

questions.rationale: Lochia rubra is the red, blood-stained discharge that occurs during the early days after childbirth. It gradually changes to lochia serosa and later lochia alba as uterine healing progresses.

questions.question_text: Which hormone is primarily responsible for milk ejection during breastfeeding?

choices.text: Oestrogen
Progesterone
Oxytocin
Follicle-stimulating hormone

questions.rationale: Oxytocin causes contraction of the myoepithelial cells surrounding the mammary alveoli, producing the milk-ejection reflex. Prolactin is primarily responsible for stimulating milk production.

questions.question_text: Which clinical finding is characteristic of pre-eclampsia?

choices.text: New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks of gestation with proteinuria and/or evidence of maternal organ dysfunction
Hypotension before 12 weeks of gestation
Isolated maternal fever without hypertension
Persistent hypoglycaemia without other abnormalities

questions.rationale: Pre-eclampsia is a pregnancy-specific hypertensive disorder characterised by new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria and/or other maternal organ dysfunction. Proteinuria is not essential when other qualifying features of organ dysfunction are present.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most common cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage?

choices.text: Uterine atony
Maternal hypoglycaemia
Neonatal hypothermia
Maternal urinary tract infection

questions.rationale: Uterine atony occurs when the uterus fails to contract adequately after childbirth. Inadequate contraction allows continued bleeding from the placental implantation site and is a major cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage.

questions.question_text: Which manoeuvre is commonly used as an initial intervention for shoulder dystocia?

choices.text: McRoberts manoeuvre
Fundal pressure
Kristeller manoeuvre
Routine forceful traction on the fetal head

questions.rationale: The McRoberts manoeuvre involves hyperflexion of the maternal hips to straighten the lumbosacral angle and facilitate release of the impacted shoulder. Fundal pressure and excessive traction on the fetal head should be avoided because they can cause serious injury.

questions.question_text: What is the major danger associated with umbilical cord prolapse?

choices.text: Maternal anaemia caused by iron deficiency
Compression of the umbilical cord resulting in reduced fetal oxygen supply
Increased maternal milk production
Premature separation of the placenta in every case

questions.rationale: Cord prolapse can result in compression of the umbilical vessels between the presenting part and maternal pelvis. This can rapidly reduce fetal oxygen delivery and cause severe fetal hypoxia or death.

questions.question_text: Which combination of findings is most suggestive of puerperal sepsis?

choices.text: Fever, uterine tenderness and offensive-smelling lochia
Mild afterpains and normal lochia
Increased appetite and normal temperature
Breast fullness without fever or systemic symptoms

questions.rationale: Puerperal sepsis is an infection of the genital tract occurring after childbirth and may present with fever, uterine tenderness and offensive lochia. Prompt recognition and treatment are essential to prevent progression to severe sepsis.

questions.question_text: Which feature best distinguishes postpartum depression from the transient postpartum blues?

choices.text: Postpartum depression involves persistent depressive symptoms that impair functioning and require clinical assessment
Postpartum depression always resolves within 24 hours
Postpartum depression occurs only during pregnancy
Postpartum depression is a normal and harmless response that never requires treatment

questions.rationale: Postpartum depression involves more persistent and clinically significant depressive symptoms than the usually short-lived postpartum blues. It can affect maternal functioning and bonding and requires appropriate assessment and support.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks attends a district hospital with severe headache, blurred vision and swelling of the face. What should the midwife do first?

choices.text: Reassure her that facial swelling is always normal in pregnancy
Assess her blood pressure and urgently evaluate for pre-eclampsia
Advise her to reduce water intake and return next week
Give routine iron tablets and discharge her

questions.rationale: Severe headache and visual disturbances are warning symptoms of possible severe pre-eclampsia. Immediate blood pressure measurement and assessment for maternal organ involvement are necessary, followed by urgent management or referral according to findings.

questions.question_text: A primigravida at 34 weeks reports that she has not felt fetal movements since the previous evening. What is the most appropriate action?

choices.text: Advise her to wait another 24 hours before seeking care
Arrange prompt assessment of fetal wellbeing
Explain that fetal movements normally stop near term
Recommend routine exercise to stimulate fetal movement without assessment

questions.rationale: A significant reduction or absence of fetal movement may indicate fetal compromise. The woman should receive prompt assessment, including fetal heart rate evaluation and further investigations or referral as clinically indicated.

questions.question_text: During antenatal screening, a pregnant woman tests positive for syphilis. Which management approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Delay treatment until after delivery
Arrange prompt treatment with the recommended penicillin regimen and partner management according to national guidance
Treat only if the woman develops a skin rash
Advise the woman to stop attending antenatal clinic

questions.rationale: Untreated maternal syphilis can cause serious fetal and neonatal complications, including congenital syphilis and stillbirth. Penicillin is the recommended treatment during pregnancy, with appropriate partner management and follow-up testing.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 28 weeks has a haemoglobin level of 8.5 g/dL and reports fatigue. Which action is most appropriate?

choices.text: Assess the cause and severity of anaemia and initiate appropriate treatment and follow-up
Reassure her that anaemia is always harmless during pregnancy
Advise her to stop taking all antenatal supplements
Wait until labour before repeating the haemoglobin test

questions.rationale: A haemoglobin level of 8.5 g/dL indicates clinically significant anaemia requiring assessment and management. The midwife should support appropriate treatment, investigate possible causes and arrange follow-up to monitor the response.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman attending a CHPS facility has a positive HIV test result. Which intervention is most appropriate?

choices.text: Advise her to avoid all antenatal care
Link her promptly to the prevention of mother-to-child transmission programme and lifelong antiretroviral therapy services
Wait until the newborn is delivered before discussing treatment
Recommend that she breastfeeds without receiving any HIV-related counselling or treatment

questions.rationale: Prompt linkage to HIV treatment and PMTCT services reduces the risk of vertical transmission and improves maternal health. Care includes antiretroviral therapy, viral load monitoring, infant prophylaxis and appropriate infant testing and feeding counselling under national guidance.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour has a cervical dilatation of 6 cm, regular contractions and reassuring fetal heart rate findings. Which action is most appropriate?

choices.text: Continue appropriate labour monitoring and provide supportive care
Perform immediate caesarean section because the cervix is not fully dilated
Stop monitoring the fetal heart rate
Administer oxytocin routinely to every woman at 6 cm

questions.rationale: A cervical dilatation of 6 cm is generally within the active phase of the first stage of labour. When maternal and fetal findings are reassuring, continued monitoring and supportive care are appropriate, with intervention guided by clinical indications.

questions.question_text: A midwife is monitoring a woman in labour using the approved labour monitoring chart. Which finding requires prompt reassessment and possible escalation?

choices.text: A reassuring fetal heart rate and progressive cervical dilatation
Persistent abnormal fetal heart rate findings
Maternal comfort between contractions
Normal maternal vital signs

questions.rationale: Persistent abnormal fetal heart rate findings may indicate fetal compromise and require urgent assessment. The midwife should evaluate the clinical situation, initiate appropriate measures and escalate care without delay.

questions.question_text: A woman has delivered her baby, and the placenta has not yet been expelled. Which action is appropriate during the third stage of labour?

choices.text: Apply controlled cord traction only when appropriate signs of placental separation are present and a skilled attendant is providing uterine support
Pull forcefully on the umbilical cord immediately after birth
Apply fundal pressure to force the placenta out
Ask the mother to stand and walk immediately

questions.rationale: Controlled cord traction is performed by a skilled attendant with appropriate uterine countertraction and after signs of placental separation. Forceful traction or fundal pressure can cause uterine inversion and serious haemorrhage.

questions.question_text: A woman in the second stage of labour has a fully dilated cervix and the fetal head is visible at the perineum. Which action is most appropriate?

choices.text: Provide supportive care, monitor fetal wellbeing and assist controlled birth of the head
Apply forceful fundal pressure
Perform routine episiotomy in every woman
Ask the woman to stop all breathing efforts until the placenta is delivered

questions.rationale: The midwife should support the woman and facilitate a controlled birth while monitoring maternal and fetal wellbeing. Episiotomy is not routine and should be performed only when clinically indicated and with appropriate consent and analgesia.

questions.question_text: A woman delivers a baby who is not breathing or crying. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Begin Helping Babies Breathe initial steps promptly, including drying, stimulation and assessment of breathing
Wait for five minutes to see whether the baby starts breathing
Give oral fluids to stimulate breathing
Place the baby in a cold environment to stimulate respiration

questions.rationale: A newborn who is not breathing or crying requires immediate assessment and initial resuscitation steps according to Helping Babies Breathe principles. If the baby remains apnoeic or gasping after the initial steps, positive-pressure ventilation should be initiated promptly according to the algorithm.

questions.question_text: Two hours after delivery, a woman has a soft uterus and heavy vaginal bleeding. What should the midwife do first?

choices.text: Recognise possible uterine atony, call for assistance and initiate immediate postpartum haemorrhage management
Wait until the next routine observation
Encourage the woman to walk around
Provide routine discharge education

questions.rationale: A soft uterus with heavy bleeding strongly suggests uterine atony, a major cause of postpartum haemorrhage. Immediate emergency response, uterine massage where indicated, uterotonic treatment according to protocol and resuscitative measures are required.

questions.question_text: A postpartum woman asks how she can know whether her newborn is attaching correctly during breastfeeding. Which observation should the midwife explain?

choices.text: The baby's mouth is wide open, the chin touches the breast and more areola is visible above the upper lip than below
The baby's lips are tucked inward and only the nipple is in the mouth
The baby makes clicking sounds throughout every feed
The mother experiences severe persistent nipple pain during the entire feed

questions.rationale: A deep attachment is indicated by a wide-open mouth, chin touching the breast and an effective latch with more areola visible above the upper lip. Poor attachment may cause nipple trauma and ineffective milk transfer.

questions.question_text: A woman on the second day after delivery has red lochia without offensive odour, fever or excessive bleeding. What is the most appropriate response?

choices.text: Explain that lochia rubra can be a normal finding during the early postpartum period
Diagnose puerperal sepsis immediately
Advise her to stop breastfeeding
Arrange emergency surgery solely because the discharge is red

questions.rationale: Lochia rubra is normally present during the early postpartum period and consists of blood-stained discharge. The midwife should continue monitoring and explain that heavy bleeding, offensive odour, fever or increasing pain requires prompt assessment.

questions.question_text: A breastfeeding mother wishes to begin contraception before discharge. Which advice is most appropriate?

choices.text: Discuss suitable postpartum methods, taking breastfeeding status, medical eligibility and the woman's preferences into account
Tell her that contraception is unnecessary while breastfeeding
Recommend that every breastfeeding woman use combined hormonal contraception immediately after birth
Advise her that contraception should only be discussed after one year

questions.rationale: Postpartum family planning should be individualised and offered before discharge when possible. Method selection must consider breastfeeding, postpartum timing, medical eligibility and informed choice.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 35 weeks has a blood pressure of 170/115 mmHg and severe epigastric pain. What is the most appropriate management priority?

choices.text: Urgently assess and stabilise the woman, initiate management of severe hypertension according to protocol and arrange obstetric review
Advise her to return for routine review in one week
Encourage unrestricted fluid intake without assessment
Discharge her if she has no vaginal bleeding

questions.rationale: Severe-range hypertension and epigastric pain suggest severe pre-eclampsia and possible hepatic involvement. Urgent maternal stabilisation, seizure prevention, blood pressure management and obstetric assessment are required.

questions.question_text: A woman with eclampsia develops a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. What should the midwife do first?

choices.text: Protect the woman from injury, position her safely, maintain airway support and summon emergency assistance
Insert a spoon into her mouth to prevent tongue biting
Restrain her limbs forcefully during the seizure
Give oral medication while she is convulsing

questions.rationale: During an eclamptic seizure, maternal safety and airway support are immediate priorities. The midwife should not restrain the woman or place objects in her mouth; magnesium sulphate and further emergency management should follow the approved protocol.

questions.question_text: A woman receiving magnesium sulphate for severe pre-eclampsia has a respiratory rate of 9 breaths per minute and absent patellar reflexes. What is the appropriate action?

choices.text: Continue the infusion and reassess in two hours
Stop magnesium sulphate, call for urgent assistance and prepare to administer calcium gluconate according to protocol
Increase the magnesium sulphate infusion rate
Encourage oral fluids and ambulation

questions.rationale: Respiratory depression and absent deep tendon reflexes are signs of magnesium sulphate toxicity. Stop the infusion, obtain urgent assistance, support respiration and administer the antidote according to the clinical protocol.

questions.question_text: A woman experiences heavy bleeding immediately after delivery. The uterus is enlarged and boggy. Which intervention is most appropriate?

choices.text: Initiate the postpartum haemorrhage protocol, massage the uterus and administer a recommended uterotonic as indicated
Wait for the placenta to be delivered before assessing the bleeding
Encourage the woman to stand and walk
Apply pressure to the woman's abdomen without assessing uterine tone

questions.rationale: A boggy uterus with heavy bleeding indicates likely uterine atony. Immediate uterine massage, uterotonic treatment, resuscitation and escalation according to the postpartum haemorrhage protocol are essential.

questions.question_text: A woman develops postpartum haemorrhage following vaginal delivery. Which medication is recommended as part of early treatment when indicated and available?

choices.text: Tranexamic acid given as early as possible within three hours of birth, alongside standard haemorrhage care
Aspirin as the first-line treatment for uterine atony
Warfarin to prevent further bleeding
Routine oral iron as the only emergency treatment

questions.rationale: Early tranexamic acid is recommended for treatment of postpartum haemorrhage and should be given as soon as possible within three hours of birth when indicated. It is an adjunct to, not a replacement for, uterotonics, resuscitation and treatment of the bleeding source.

questions.question_text: During delivery, the fetal head is born but retracts tightly against the maternal perineum, and the shoulders fail to deliver. What should the midwife suspect?

choices.text: Shoulder dystocia
Normal restitution
Placenta praevia
Cord presentation

questions.rationale: Retraction of the fetal head against the perineum, commonly called the turtle sign, is a recognised feature of shoulder dystocia. Immediate activation of the shoulder dystocia response and appropriate manoeuvres are required.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour has a prolapsed umbilical cord following spontaneous rupture of membranes. The fetal heart rate is slow. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Relieve pressure on the cord by elevating the presenting part, call for help and arrange urgent birth
Attempt to push the cord back into the uterus
Ask the woman to walk around to improve fetal descent
Apply fundal pressure to speed up delivery

questions.rationale: Cord prolapse with fetal bradycardia is an obstetric emergency because cord compression can rapidly cause fetal hypoxia. The presenting part should be elevated to relieve compression, emergency assistance obtained and urgent delivery arranged; the cord should not be handled or pushed back unnecessarily.

questions.question_text: A woman at a district hospital has signs of obstructed labour, including severe caput formation, moulding and failure of the presenting part to descend. What is the most appropriate action?

choices.text: Continue routine labour observation for several more hours
Recognise obstructed labour, initiate appropriate stabilisation and arrange urgent referral for definitive obstetric management
Apply fundal pressure to force descent
Discharge the woman to rest at home

questions.rationale: Obstructed labour can cause uterine rupture, haemorrhage, infection and fetal compromise. The midwife should avoid harmful interventions, stabilise the woman within the facility's capacity and arrange urgent transfer to a facility capable of definitive management.

questions.question_text: A woman on the fifth day after delivery presents with fever, lower abdominal pain and offensive-smelling lochia. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Suspect puerperal infection and arrange urgent clinical assessment and treatment
Reassure her that offensive lochia is normal throughout the puerperium
Advise her to stop drinking fluids
Recommend only routine perineal washing and no further assessment

questions.rationale: Fever, abdominal pain and offensive lochia are concerning for puerperal infection, including endometritis. Prompt assessment and appropriate antimicrobial treatment are important to prevent progression to sepsis.

questions.question_text: A postpartum woman with suspected sepsis becomes confused, tachycardic and hypotensive. What is the priority action?

choices.text: Activate the emergency response, assess and support airway, breathing and circulation, and initiate urgent sepsis management
Wait for the fever to resolve without treatment
Provide routine breastfeeding education first
Discharge the woman if the vaginal bleeding has stopped

questions.rationale: Confusion, tachycardia and hypotension in a woman with suspected infection suggest possible sepsis with circulatory compromise. Immediate escalation, resuscitation, prompt antimicrobial treatment and source management are essential.

questions.question_text: A woman two weeks after childbirth reports persistent sadness, loss of interest, poor sleep even when the baby sleeps and feelings of worthlessness. What should the midwife do?

choices.text: Assess for postpartum depression and arrange appropriate mental health support
Tell her that these symptoms are always normal and require no attention
Advise her to stop breastfeeding immediately
Ignore the symptoms unless they continue for one year

questions.rationale: Persistent low mood, loss of interest and worthlessness may indicate postpartum depression rather than transient postpartum blues. The midwife should assess symptom severity, functional impact and safety, then facilitate appropriate treatment and support.

questions.question_text: A postpartum woman tells the midwife that she has thoughts of harming herself. What is the most appropriate response?

choices.text: Take the disclosure seriously, assess immediate safety and arrange urgent mental health evaluation
Tell her that mothers should never express such thoughts
Leave her alone to give her time to think
Advise her to avoid discussing the issue with healthcare professionals

questions.rationale: Thoughts of self-harm require immediate risk assessment and appropriate urgent intervention. The woman should not be left without appropriate support and supervision while safety arrangements and specialist assessment are organised.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour has been receiving continuous support. Her contractions are strong, but cervical dilatation has not progressed and the fetal head remains high. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

choices.text: Possible labour dystocia requiring reassessment of contractions, fetal position and maternal pelvis
Normal progress that requires no further assessment
Evidence that the placenta has separated
Proof that the woman is in the third stage of labour

questions.rationale: Strong contractions without cervical progress or descent may indicate labour dystocia. The midwife should reassess the woman and fetus, identify possible contributing factors and seek appropriate obstetric review.

questions.question_text: A woman at 36 weeks has a blood pressure of 168/112 mmHg, severe headache and visual disturbances. While awaiting urgent obstetric review, she develops a generalised seizure. Which action should take priority?

choices.text: Protect her from injury, maintain airway support, summon emergency assistance and initiate eclampsia management
Attempt to complete a routine antenatal examination
Give oral antihypertensive medication while she is convulsing
Wait for the seizure to recur before starting treatment

questions.rationale: The woman has progressed from severe pre-eclampsia to eclampsia, which is a life-threatening emergency. Maternal safety, airway support, magnesium sulphate treatment according to protocol and urgent obstetric management take priority.

questions.question_text: Following delivery, a woman has persistent heavy bleeding. The uterus is firm and well contracted, but examination reveals a deep vaginal laceration. Which cause of postpartum haemorrhage is most likely?

choices.text: Trauma to the genital tract
Uterine atony
Retained urine
Normal uterine involution

questions.rationale: Persistent bleeding with a firm, contracted uterus suggests a cause other than uterine atony. A vaginal or cervical laceration is a traumatic cause of postpartum haemorrhage and requires prompt examination and repair by an appropriately skilled clinician.

questions.question_text: During a vaginal birth, shoulder dystocia is diagnosed. The midwife performs the McRoberts manoeuvre and applies suprapubic pressure, but the shoulder remains impacted. What should happen next?

choices.text: Continue the emergency shoulder dystocia algorithm, call for additional skilled assistance and use appropriate further manoeuvres
Apply strong fundal pressure
Apply forceful downward traction to the fetal head
Stop all assistance and wait for spontaneous delivery

questions.rationale: Failure of initial manoeuvres requires prompt progression through the established shoulder dystocia algorithm with additional skilled assistance. Fundal pressure and excessive traction on the fetal head can worsen impaction and cause maternal or neonatal injury.

questions.question_text: A woman with a previous caesarean section is in labour. She suddenly develops severe continuous abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, maternal tachycardia and fetal bradycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.text: Uterine rupture
Normal transition phase of labour
Uncomplicated Braxton Hicks contractions
Physiological postpartum involution

questions.rationale: Previous uterine surgery increases the risk of uterine rupture during labour. Sudden continuous pain, bleeding, maternal instability and fetal bradycardia are highly concerning findings requiring immediate emergency obstetric intervention.

questions.question_text: A woman on the third day after caesarean section has a temperature of 39°C, wound discharge, increasing abdominal pain and tachycardia. Which clinical decision is most appropriate?

choices.text: Suspect postoperative infection with possible puerperal sepsis and initiate urgent assessment and treatment
Assume the symptoms are normal effects of surgery
Discharge the woman because the operation has been completed
Treat only the wound discharge without assessing for systemic infection

questions.rationale: Fever, wound discharge, abdominal pain and tachycardia suggest postoperative infection and possible sepsis. The woman requires urgent assessment, appropriate investigations, antimicrobial treatment and source control as indicated.

questions.question_text: A woman ten days after childbirth reports that she hears voices instructing her to harm her newborn. She appears confused and expresses unusual beliefs about the baby. What is the most appropriate action?

choices.text: Suspect postpartum psychosis, ensure immediate safety of mother and baby, and arrange emergency specialist assessment
Reassure her that this is ordinary postpartum blues
Leave her alone with the newborn to encourage bonding
Delay assessment until the routine six-week postnatal visit

questions.rationale: Hallucinations, unusual beliefs and confusion in the postpartum period may indicate postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency. Immediate safety measures and urgent specialist assessment are essential because there may be a risk of harm to the mother or newborn.

questions.question_text: A woman in labour has a persistently abnormal fetal heart rate, increasing maternal pulse and a labour monitoring chart showing poor progress. The district hospital has no emergency operative delivery capacity. Which decision best reduces the risk of maternal and perinatal mortality?

choices.text: Continue observation until the fetal heart rate becomes absent
Recognise possible fetal compromise and labour dystocia, stabilise the woman and arrange urgent referral to a facility with operative capacity
Discharge the woman to seek care elsewhere independently
Wait until the end of the shift to contact the receiving hospital

questions.rationale: Persistent fetal heart rate abnormalities with poor labour progress may indicate serious fetal compromise and require urgent intervention. Timely recognition, stabilisation, communication with the receiving facility and organised referral are essential when the current facility lacks definitive treatment capacity.

questions.question_text: A woman on the fourth postpartum day reports increasing vaginal bleeding, passes large clots and feels dizzy. Which interpretation and action are most appropriate?

choices.text: Possible secondary postpartum haemorrhage requiring urgent assessment and management
Normal lochia alba requiring no assessment
Normal uterine involution that should be ignored
A normal sign that breastfeeding is well established

questions.rationale: Increasing bleeding and passage of large clots after the first 24 hours may indicate secondary postpartum haemorrhage. Dizziness raises concern about significant blood loss, so urgent assessment for causes such as retained placental tissue or infection is required.

questions.question_text: A woman develops postpartum haemorrhage following delivery. Despite uterine massage and uterotonic treatment, bleeding continues and she becomes hypotensive. What is the most appropriate next course of action?

choices.text: Continue routine observation because uterotonics have already been administered
Escalate immediately for advanced haemorrhage management, resuscitation and definitive control of the bleeding source
Stop intravenous access to reduce blood loss
Delay further intervention until the woman loses consciousness

questions.rationale: Persistent bleeding with hypotension indicates ongoing haemorrhage and possible haemorrhagic shock despite initial treatment. Immediate escalation, blood product support when indicated and definitive interventions to control the source of bleeding are required.

questions.question_text: A pregnant woman at 37 weeks presents with painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding. Her vital signs are currently stable, and the presenting part is high. Which action is most appropriate?

choices.text: Perform a digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation
Suspect placenta praevia, avoid digital vaginal examination and arrange urgent obstetric assessment
Encourage immediate pushing to deliver the baby
Discharge her because she is not yet in labour

questions.rationale: Painless bright-red bleeding with a high presenting part raises suspicion of placenta praevia. Digital vaginal examination must be avoided until placenta praevia has been excluded because it may precipitate severe haemorrhage.
